professionalScope.en: Continuing professional education for licensed clinicians and allied providers. Every learner gets the same evidence, regulatory status and safety content; what each may do with it — prescribe, recommend, administer, or refer — follows their own licence and scope, and the course adapts its practice guidance to that role. It informs clinical reasoning; it is not a protocol, contains no dosing, and does not replace specialist input, formal guidelines or individual judgment.

disclaimers.en: Educational content for clinicians. It does not prescribe, and it never restates an evidence grade above what the source assigns to the specific indication.

Regulatory statements name their jurisdiction and date. US status (FDA, 503A/503B compounding) is given in the lesson text; status in the United Kingdom, the European Union, Portugal, Brazil and the United Arab Emirates (federal, with Dubai and Abu Dhabi where they differ) is given in each moment's regulatory note, read from each regulator's own primary sources in September 2026, and the learner's own country is shown first. The US compounding categories have no equivalent in the other jurisdictions. Check the live status with the national regulator before acting.
Designed toward future CME accreditation. No CME or CE credit is currently offered.

claims.text: In the UAE, the Emirates Drug Establishment (EDE; 'UAE Drug Corporation' in the official English translation) has been the federal authority regulating medical products since Federal Decree-Law 28/2023 (issued 25 Sep 2023, in force 30 Sep 2023), with the power to approve and register medical products.

refs.title: Federal Decree-Law No. (28) of 2023 On the Establishment of the UAE Drug Corporation (official English translation)
refs.publication: UAE Legislations portal; Official Gazette No. 760 (29 Sep 2023)

claims.text: In the UAE, since 2 January 2025 (Federal Decree-Law 38/2024, which replaced Federal Law 8/2019), no medical product may be imported, distributed, possessed, sold, displayed, used or manufactured for circulation without an EDE marketing approval.

refs.title: Federal Decree-Law No. (38) of 2024 Governing Medical Products, Pharmacists and Pharmaceutical Establishments (official English translation)
refs.publication: UAE Legislations portal; Official Gazette No. 785 (14 Oct 2024)

claims.text: In the UAE, physicians may prescribe a medicine for uses not in its leaflet, or a medicine never submitted for marketing approval, only when necessary, when no equivalent alternative is available and with the patient's approval; compassionate use is excluded from this rule (Federal Decree-Law 38/2024, Art. 42(1)).

refs.title: Federal Decree-Law No. (38) of 2024 Governing Medical Products, Pharmacists and Pharmaceutical Establishments (official English translation)
refs.publication: UAE Legislations portal; Official Gazette No. 785 (14 Oct 2024)

claims.text: In Dubai, the DHA prohibits circulating, prescribing, dispensing, administering or using any peptide product unless it is registered or licensed with the EDE and used within the scope of its licence, and requires registered peptide products to be used strictly within their approved indications (External Circular 0867, 29 July 2026).

refs.title: DHA External Circular DHA/OUT/2026/0000867: Regulations for Handling Peptide Products in Healthcare Facilities (technical annex)

claims.text: In the UAE, medical products compounded in licensed compounding pharmacies are exempt from the marketing-approval requirement (Federal Decree-Law 38/2024, Art. 5(2), in force 2 Jan 2025).

refs.title: Federal Decree-Law No. (38) of 2024 Governing Medical Products, Pharmacists and Pharmaceutical Establishments (official English translation)
refs.publication: UAE Legislations portal; Official Gazette No. 785 (14 Oct 2024)

claims.text: In the UAE, a compounding pharmacy may not compound essential copies of products holding an EDE marketing approval unless no commercially available product can deliver the expected benefit to the patient, and may not formulate products intended for research, development or experimentation (Federal Decree-Law 38/2024, Art. 95).

refs.title: Federal Decree-Law No. (38) of 2024 Governing Medical Products, Pharmacists and Pharmaceutical Establishments (official English translation)
refs.publication: UAE Legislations portal; Official Gazette No. 785 (14 Oct 2024)

claims.text: In Abu Dhabi, the DoH Standard for Provision of Compounding Pharmacy Services (August 2026) allows compounding only for a genuine, documented clinical need that no suitable licensed product meets, and bars copying commercially available products for convenience or cost or introducing experimental or unverified products.

refs.title: DoH Standard for Provision of Compounding Pharmacy Services (DoH/SD/HLS/PCPS/V1/2026)
refs.publication: DoH standard; published and effective August 2026

claims.text: In Abu Dhabi, compounding requires a Good Compounding Practice (GCP) certificate issued by the EDE, and compounding from unapproved or unknown-source substances, or from substances not on the DoH Registry for Compounded Substances, is prohibited unless the DoH permits it (DoH compounding standard, August 2026).

refs.title: DoH Standard for Provision of Compounding Pharmacy Services (DoH/SD/HLS/PCPS/V1/2026)
refs.publication: DoH standard; published and effective August 2026

claims.text: In Abu Dhabi, the DoH treats peptides as emerging, non-monographed, high-risk substances: novel substances of unknown risk may be compounded only if monographed, a component of an approved medicine, or listed on the DoH Registry for Compounded Substances (DoH compounding standard, August 2026).

refs.title: DoH Standard for Provision of Compounding Pharmacy Services (DoH/SD/HLS/PCPS/V1/2026)
refs.publication: DoH standard; published and effective August 2026

claims.text: In Abu Dhabi, where emerging substances such as peptides are permitted, prescribing is limited to eligible facilities and credentialed prescribers for accepted indications, office-stock ordering to hospitals and DoH-approved specialty clinics, and compounding pharmacies must dispense only against individual prescriptions (DoH compounding standard, August 2026).

refs.title: DoH Standard for Provision of Compounding Pharmacy Services (DoH/SD/HLS/PCPS/V1/2026)
refs.publication: DoH standard; published and effective August 2026

claims.text: In Abu Dhabi, compounded peptide formulations may use only certified active ingredients imported under EDE oversight, clinics must hold technical agreements with licensed compounding pharmacies, and peptide products must be traceable from source to patient (DoH Circular 148/2026, 31 July 2026).

refs.title: DoH Circular No. (148)/2026: Mandatory Requirements for Peptide Products

claims.text: In Dubai, the DHA prohibits using any peptide product intended for research use on humans or for therapeutic purposes outside a study or clinical trial approved by the competent authority (External Circular 0867, 29 July 2026).

refs.title: DHA External Circular DHA/OUT/2026/0000867: Regulations for Handling Peptide Products in Healthcare Facilities (technical annex)

claims.text: In Dubai, facilities may not buy, accept or use peptide products from websites, social media, individual accounts or unlicensed or unverifiable suppliers, and products without full identification data (active substance, concentration, batch, expiry) may not be used (DHA External Circular 0867, 29 July 2026).

refs.title: DHA External Circular DHA/OUT/2026/0000867: Regulations for Handling Peptide Products in Healthcare Facilities (technical annex)

claims.text: In the UAE, Federal Decree-Law 38/2024 brings cosmetics with a medical effect on the skin, hair or nails within its definition of medical products regulated by the EDE.

refs.title: Federal Decree-Law No. (38) of 2024 Governing Medical Products, Pharmacists and Pharmaceutical Establishments (official English translation)

claims.text: In the UAE, the EDE registers 'healthcare products' not intended to diagnose, treat or prevent disease, including dietary supplements, herbal products and cosmetics with a medical effect, through a marketing authorisation valid for five years (EDE service page, read 25 Sep 2026).

refs.title: Issuance of Marketing Authorization for a Healthcare Product (service page)

claims.text: In the UAE, whether a borderline product (for example a peptide serum) needs an EDE marketing authorisation, and in which category, is settled by an EDE classification letter based on the product's presentation, composition, use and design (EDE service page, read 25 Sep 2026).

refs.title: Classification of a Medical Product (service page)

claims.text: In the UAE, ordinary cosmetics and personal-care products are a MoIAT-regulated product category under Cabinet Resolution 18/2014 (the UAE control system for cosmetics and personal care products), needing a conformity certificate backed by accredited test reports, a formula declaration and a product safety report.

refs.title: قائمة بمتطلبات جميع التشريعات و الأنظمة الرقابية الخاصة بالمنتجات (List of technical requirements for regulated products, 'CAD Regulated Sheet')

claims.text: In Abu Dhabi, the DoH classes topical cosmetic peptides with no systemic effect as low-risk products that stay under existing regulatory pathways, while systemic, regenerative or weakly evidenced peptides face enhanced controls (Circular 148/2026, 31 July 2026).

refs.title: DoH Circular No. (148)/2026: Mandatory Requirements for Peptide Products

claims.text: In the UAE, food supplements are medical products under Federal Decree-Law 38/2024, defined as oral products that support the diet and do not treat, diagnose or prevent disease.

refs.title: Federal Decree-Law No. (38) of 2024 Governing Medical Products, Pharmacists and Pharmaceutical Establishments (official English translation)
refs.publication: UAE Legislations portal; Official Gazette No. 785 (14 Oct 2024)

claims.text: In the UAE, advertising or promoting any medical product by any means, including social media, requires EDE approval, and advertising controlled or semi-controlled products to the public is prohibited (Federal Decree-Law 38/2024, Art. 44).

refs.title: Federal Decree-Law No. (38) of 2024 Governing Medical Products, Pharmacists and Pharmaceutical Establishments (official English translation)
refs.publication: UAE Legislations portal; Official Gazette No. 785 (14 Oct 2024)

claims.text: In the UAE, an EDE licence to advertise a medical product requires a valid EDE marketing authorisation for the product (only products exempted by the Cabinet under Art. 5(3) of Federal Decree-Law 38/2024 are excused), a licensed pharmaceutical or healthcare establishment as applicant, and truthful, evidence-based content matching the approved indications (EDE service page, read 25 Sep 2026).

refs.title: Licensing an advertisement for a medical product (service page)

claims.text: In Dubai, the DHA bans misleading or unproven peptide claims, including anti-aging, cell regeneration, weight loss, muscle building and improved appearance, unless the use is within the product's approved status, and requires any promotion of unregistered materials, including through influencers or social media, to stop (29 July 2026).

refs.title: DHA External Circular DHA/OUT/2026/0000867: Regulations for Handling Peptide Products in Healthcare Facilities (technical annex)

claims.text: In Abu Dhabi, healthcare providers may not promote peptide therapies with misleading or unsubstantiated claims, or advertise, market or publish media content about them without prior approval from the DoH and relevant authorities (Circular 148/2026, 31 July 2026).

refs.title: DoH Circular No. (148)/2026: Mandatory Requirements for Peptide Products

claims.text: In Abu Dhabi, emerging and non-monographed compounded substances such as peptides may not be advertised, promoted or marketed, directly or indirectly, to patients or healthcare professionals (DoH compounding standard, August 2026).

refs.title: DoH Standard for Provision of Compounding Pharmacy Services (DoH/SD/HLS/PCPS/V1/2026)
refs.publication: DoH standard; published and effective August 2026

claims.text: In Dubai, peptide products may be prescribed, dispensed or administered only by licensed, authorised professionals in a licensed facility, and injections or IV therapies for 'wellness', 'recovery', 'detoxification' or 'energy enhancement' are not permitted without a documented medical indication and treatment plan (DHA External Circular 0867, 29 July 2026).

refs.title: DHA External Circular DHA/OUT/2026/0000867: Regulations for Handling Peptide Products in Healthcare Facilities (technical annex)

claims.text: In Abu Dhabi, physicians may prescribe peptide therapies only for clinical indications supported by available scientific evidence, after a documented eligibility assessment and with informed consent that covers benefits, uncertainties, risks, alternatives and the product's regulatory approval status (DoH Circular 148/2026, 31 July 2026).

refs.title: DoH Circular No. (148)/2026: Mandatory Requirements for Peptide Products

claims.text: The skin works as a peripheral neuro-immuno-endocrine organ: reviews describe four immuno-endocrine units (epidermal, dermal, hypodermal, adnexal) whose cells make and respond to hormones and signal to neighbouring cells, through sensory nerves, and through the circulation. This is a mechanistic framework drawn from cell, tissue and animal work.

claims.text: Skin cells carry the enzymes to make steroids from cholesterol (CYP11A1) and to activate circulating precursors (11β-HSD1, 5α-reductase, aromatase), producing cortisol, DHT and estradiol locally; this rests mainly on cell, tissue and biochemical studies.

refs.title: Keratinocytes control skin immune homeostasis through de novo-synthesized glucocorticoids

claims.text: The skin also runs shortened thyroid-like (TRH, TSH, deiodinase-generated T3) and somatotropic (GH/IGF-1) loops; the thyroid-like evidence comes mainly from mouse models and the follicle GH/IGF-1 loop from human follicles ex vivo.

claims.text: Systemic hormones act on skin (body-to-skin): cortisol excess thins the dermis and causes striae and bruising; hypothyroidism gives dry, coarse skin and myxoedema. The Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide treats the aesthetic exam as a systemic screen and lists suspected Cushing syndrome (violaceous striae, central obesity, proximal weakness, new hypertension or diabetes) and rapidly progressive virilisation among reasons to refer promptly to endocrinology.

claims.text: The atlas's authors describe its scores as putative and hypothesis-generating, not functional hormones and receptors, and leave validation to in vitro and in vivo work; more generally, transcript levels alone often fail to predict protein levels. A transcriptomic map therefore shows capacity, not secretion or effect.

claims.text: In 178 adults of the Leiden Longevity Study, more p16-positive cells in sun-protected arm skin were associated with ageing-type elastic fibres, more facial wrinkles and higher perceived age independent of chronological age; people in the lowest tertile of epidermal p16 counts looked about 3 years younger than those in the highest. This is an association, not evidence of cause.

claims.text: Skin collagen falls with age; aged human dermis shows more fibroblast MMP-1, fragmented collagen and fibroblasts under less mechanical tension that make less procollagen, and culture work shows fragmentation feeds back to raise MMP-1. That senescent cells drive this in living skin is plausible but not shown.

claims.text: Causal evidence that senescent cells drive ageing comes from mice: clearing p16-positive cells extended healthy lifespan and senolytics improved function and survival in old mice; skin was checked only for safety (thickness, fibrosis, wound closure), and clearing p16-positive cells during healing slowed wound closure.

claims.text: Per the Endocrine Society diagnostic guideline, the features that best discriminate Cushing's syndrome are easy bruising, facial plethora, proximal myopathy and striae that are reddish-purple and wider than 1 cm; facial fullness, dorsocervical fat pad, weight gain, acne, hirsutism, thin skin and fatigue are common in the general population and less discriminatory.

claims.text: Endogenous Cushing's syndrome is uncommon (2–3 new cases per million per year in European population studies); the commonest cause of Cushing's syndrome is iatrogenic, and the guideline recommends a drug history (oral, inhaled, topical, injected — including skin-bleaching creams, herbal tonics and joint or nerve injections) before any biochemical testing.

refs.title: The diagnosis of Cushing's syndrome: an Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline

claims.text: The guideline recommends testing patients with multiple and progressive features (particularly the discriminating ones) or features unusual for age, recommends against widespread testing and against random serum cortisol, and sends abnormal results to an endocrinologist. The Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide adds that consumer cortisol panels are poorly validated and reads most popular 'cortisol face' as a lifestyle-and-fluid picture.

citations.title: Neuro-immuno-endocrinology of the skin: how environment regulates body homeostasis
citations.authors: Slominski RM, Raman C, Jetten AM, Slominski AT

note.en: narrative review · academic · role: A&RE ch.6 ref 1 — the four immuno-endocrine units (epidermal, dermal, hypodermal, adnexal) and the three routes (local, neural, circulation) · PMID 40263492 · Publisher correction PMID 40316721. Guide reference resolves exactly.

citations.title: Neuroendocrinology of the skin

note.en: narrative review · academic · role: A&RE ch.5 ref 3, ch.6 ref 3, ch.7 ref 4 — CRH, POMC, ACTH, α-MSH and β-endorphin are made in skin with their receptors (para/autocrine action); dermal and epidermal units · PMID 11041445 · Erratum 2002. Also cited by A&RE ch.7 for the estrogen–senescence statement, which this 2000 review does not address (see findings).

citations.title: The human skin as a hormone target and an endocrine gland

note.en: narrative review · academic · role: A&RE ch.5 ref 4, ch.7 ref 2 — skin makes, activates and releases hormones, including sex steroids that matter for the whole organism, especially in older people · PMID 16982574 · Verified; no PMCID.

citations.title: Neuronal control of skin function: the skin as a neuroimmunoendocrine organ
citations.authors: Roosterman D, Goerge T, Schneider SW, Bunnett NW, Steinhoff M

note.en: narrative review · academic · role: A&RE ch.5 ref 13 — sensory nerves and neuropeptides as the neural arm of the skin's signalling network · PMID 17015491 · Verified.

citations.title: Steroidogenesis in the skin: implications for local immune functions
citations.authors: Slominski A, Zbytek B, Nikolakis G, et al.

note.en: narrative review · academic · role: A&RE ch.6 ref 4 — skin cells hold the full apparatus (CYP11A1 onward) to make glucocorticoids, androgens and estrogens or activate circulating precursors; the review also describes a skin contribution to circulating androgens and estrogens · PMID 23435015 · Verified.

citations.title: Keratinocytes control skin immune homeostasis through de novo-synthesized glucocorticoids
citations.authors: Phan TS, Schink L, Mann J, et al.

note.en: mouse genetic model (keratinocyte Cyp11b1 deletion) plus human disease association · academic · role: A&RE ch.6 ref 5 — keratinocyte-made glucocorticoids restrain skin inflammation; the functional proof is in mice · PMID 33514551 · The guide presents this without naming the species; the course labels it as animal evidence.

citations.title: Human hair follicles display a functional equivalent of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis and synthesize cortisol
citations.authors: Ito N, Ito T, Kromminga A, et al.

note.en: human scalp hair follicles in organ culture (ex vivo) · academic · role: A&RE ch.6 ref 11 — CRH → POMC/ACTH → cortisol secretion with glucocorticoid feedback on CRH, in follicles with no systemic connections · PMID 15946990 · Verified.

citations.title: Human Hair Follicles Operate a Functional Peripheral Equivalent of the Hypothalamic-Pituitary-Somatotropic Axis Ex Vivo
citations.authors: Horesh EJ, Gherardini J, Alam M, et al.

note.en: research letter; human follicles ex vivo · academic · role: A&RE ch.6 ref 12 — a GH/IGF-1 loop in the follicle · PMID 36496194 · No abstract indexed and not open access; cited only for the finding its title states.

citations.title: Thyroid hormone action in epidermal development and homeostasis and its implications in the pathophysiology of the skin
citations.authors: Mancino G, Miro C, Di Cicco E, Dentice M

note.en: narrative review (mouse models of thyroid-hormone metabolism) · academic · role: A&RE ch.6 ref 7 — local deiodinase control of T3 in keratinocytes; the review says the mechanisms are being clarified mainly in mouse models · PMID 33683663 · Verified.

citations.title: Photosynthesis of previtamin D3 in human skin and the physiologic consequences
citations.authors: Holick MF, MacLaughlin JA, Clark MB, et al.

note.en: human skin photobiology · academic · role: the skin-to-body example: previtamin D3 forms in human skin under solar UV and vitamin D3 is carried into the circulation by vitamin D-binding protein · PMID 6251551 · Not cited by either guide; added as the primary for the statement that skin supplies a whole-body hormone system.

citations.title: Vitamin D metabolism, mechanism of action, and clinical applications

note.en: narrative review · academic · role: A&RE ch.7 ref 3 — vitamin D3 made in skin from 7-dehydrocholesterol, then 25(OH)D and 1,25(OH)2D elsewhere · PMID 24529992 · Verified.

citations.title: Thyroid hormone action on skin

note.en: clinical review · academic · role: A&RE ch.5 ref 8 — the skin signs of thyroid disease (myxoedema; dry, coarse skin) · PMID 22110782 · Verified (a 2012 review with the same title exists, PMID 22914563; the guide's volume and pages match this one).

citations.title: A Hormone Cell Atlas maps the human endocrine system at cellular resolution
citations.authors: Fei L, Huang-Doran I, Lawler K, et al. (senior authors Teichmann SA, Farooqi IS)

note.en: single-cell and single-nucleus transcriptomic atlas (hormone2cell): 379 hormone and receptor genes, ~14 million cells and nuclei, 47 human tissues · academic (University of Cambridge, Wellcome Sanger Institute) · role: A&RE ch.7 ref 1 — predicted hormone-producing and hormone-receiving cell types; the transcriptomic map the lesson is about · PMID 42207862 · PubMed entry 2026-05-28 (the guide's 'published online May 28, 2026'); print issue 2 Jul 2026. Full text and supplement paywalled (HTTP 403); only abstract- and portal-level facts are taught.

citations.title: Hormone Cell Atlas portal — About and FAQs
citations.authors: Hormone Cell Atlas team (Farooqi and Teichmann groups)

note.en: data portal · atlas authors · role: the authors' own usage statement: predictions are 'putative and hypothesis-generating, rather than … functional hormones and receptors', validation is the user's responsibility; 47 disease-free tissues, 1,900+ cell types, 14 million+ cells; skin is listed among the tissues on the sister cellxgene site (hormonecellatlas.cellgeni.sanger.ac.uk) · Fetched live 2026-09-24 (HTTP 200).

citations.title: On the Dependency of Cellular Protein Levels on mRNA Abundance
citations.authors: Liu Y, Beyer A, Aebersold R

note.en: narrative review · academic · role: transcript levels by themselves are not sufficient to predict protein levels in many scenarios · PMID 27104977 · Not cited by either guide; added to support the RNA-versus-protein step.

citations.title: The effect of sunscreen on vitamin D: a review
citations.authors: Neale RE, Khan SR, Lucas RM, Waterhouse M, Whiteman DC, Olsen CM

note.en: systematic review (MOOSE): 4 experimental studies, 3 field trials (2 RCTs), 69 observational studies · academic (QIMR Berghofer, Australian National University) · role: tests the guide's pearl that serum 25(OH)D falls with sunscreen use: experiments with artificial UV show a block; randomized field trials of daily sunscreen (SPF ~16) show no fall; high-SPF products untested · PMID 30945275 · Not cited by either guide; contradicts A&RE ch.7 testing pearl (see findings).

citations.title: Senescence-associated secretory phenotypes reveal cell-nonautonomous functions of oncogenic RAS and the p53 tumor suppressor
citations.authors: Coppé JP, Patil CK, Rodier F, et al.

note.en: cultured human fibroblasts and epithelial cells after genotoxic stress (+ prostate tumours after chemotherapy) · academic · role: defines the SASP (IL-6, IL-8 and other secreted factors) — the concept the guide uses · PMID 19053174 · Not cited by either guide; the primary behind 'SASP'.

citations.title: p16INK4A is a robust in vivo biomarker of cellular aging in human skin
citations.authors: Ressler S, Bartkova J, Niederegger H, et al.

note.en: human skin tissue bank, cross-sectional (0–20, 21–70, 71–95 years) · academic · role: p16-positive cells are more numerous in older skin, in both epidermis and dermis · PMID 16911562 · Not cited by either guide.

citations.title: P16INK4a Positive Cells in Human Skin Are Indicative of Local Elastic Fiber Morphology, Facial Wrinkling, and Perceived Age
citations.authors: Waaijer ME, Gunn DA, Adams PD, et al.
citations.publication: J Gerontol A Biol Sci Med Sci · 2016;71:1022–1028

note.en: cohort (Leiden Longevity Study), n=178, aged 45–81, sun-protected upper-inner-arm biopsies · academic; one co-author from Unilever; NIH and Cancer Research UK grants · role: senescent-cell counts in human skin track with elastic-fibre changes, facial wrinkles and perceived age, independent of chronological age; lowest vs highest tertile of epidermal p16 counts looked ~3 years younger · PMID 26286607 · Not cited by either guide.

citations.title: Faces of cellular senescence in skin aging

note.en: narrative review · academic · role: A&RE ch.7 ref 5 — senescent cells accumulate in several human skin compartments; cell types respond differently · PMID 34166688 · Verified.

citations.title: Biomarkers of Cellular Senescence and Skin Aging

note.en: narrative review · academic · role: A&RE ch.7 ref 6 — no universal biomarker identifies senescent cells unequivocally; markers by skin compartment · PMID 30190724 · Full text (PMC6115505) read: it does not discuss estrogen loss or hormone responsiveness, which A&RE ch.7 cites it for.

citations.title: Targeting cellular senescence in dermatology: senolytic and senomorphic strategies
citations.authors: Haykal D, Flament F, Garibyan L, Lee K, Escot J, Gueniche A, Kirkland J

note.en: narrative review (no new data) · three authors from L'Oréal and a senolytic-field investigator; declares no competing interests · role: how dermatologic senotherapy stands in 2026: a review of mechanism and prospects; transient senescence aids wound repair · PMID 42417965 · Not cited by either guide.

citations.title: The influence of age and sex on skin thickness, skin collagen and density
citations.authors: Shuster S, Black MM, McVitie E

note.en: cross-sectional reference measurements of forearm skin · academic · role: A&RE ch.5 ref 1 — skin collagen falls with age and is lower in women at all ages · PMID 1220811 · The abstract gives no annual rate; the guide's '~1% per year' could not be checked and is not taught.

citations.title: Decreased collagen production in chronologically aged skin: roles of age-dependent alteration in fibroblast function and defective mechanical stimulation
citations.authors: Varani J, Dame MK, Rittie L, et al.

note.en: human skin sections (18–29 vs 80+ years) and isolated dermal fibroblasts · academic · role: aged fibroblasts make less procollagen and are less attached to and stretched by collagen — two routes to lower synthesis · PMID 16723701 · Not cited by either guide.

citations.title: Collagen fragmentation promotes oxidative stress and elevates matrix metalloproteinase-1 in fibroblasts in aged human skin
citations.authors: Fisher GJ, Quan T, Purohit T, et al.

note.en: aged (>80) vs young (21–30) human skin in vivo, plus organ and collagen-lattice culture · academic · role: more fibroblast MMP-1 in aged human dermis; fragmented collagen lowers fibroblast stretch and raises MMP-1 and oxidants — a self-perpetuating loop · PMID 19116368 · Not cited by either guide.

citations.title: Mechanisms of photoaging and chronological skin aging
citations.authors: Fisher GJ, Kang S, Varani J, et al.

note.en: narrative review with new data · academic · role: A&RE ch.5 ref 2 — UV drives the matrix breakdown of photoageing, and photoageing and chronological ageing share molecular pathways · PMID 12437452 · Verified.

citations.title: Naturally occurring p16(Ink4a)-positive cells shorten healthy lifespan
citations.authors: Baker DJ, Childs BG, Durik M, et al.

note.en: mouse (INK-ATTAC transgene) · academic · role: A&RE ch.13 ref 2 — clearing p16-positive cells from one year of age extended median lifespan and delayed kidney, heart and fat deterioration; skin was checked for safety only (thickness, fibrosis), and clearance during healing slowed wound closure (Extended Data Fig. 10) · PMID 26840489 · Verified.

citations.title: Senolytics improve physical function and increase lifespan in old age
citations.authors: Xu M, Pirtskhalava T, Farr JN, et al.

note.en: mouse, plus human adipose-tissue explants · several authors hold a financial interest; Mayo Clinic holds senolytic patents · role: A&RE ch.17 ref 1 — senescent cells cause dysfunction when transplanted; senolytics improved function and post-treatment survival in old mice · PMID 29988130 · Verified.

citations.title: Senolytics decrease senescent cells in humans: Preliminary report from a clinical trial of Dasatinib plus Quercetin in individuals with diabetic kidney disease
citations.authors: Hickson LJ, Langhi Prata LGP, Bobart SA, et al.

note.en: open-label phase 1 pilot, n=9, diabetic kidney disease (NCT02848131) · investigators with a financial interest; Mayo Clinic holds patents · role: A&RE ch.17 ref 3 — after a short course, epidermal p16- and p21-positive cells and circulating SASP factors fell; tissue-marker endpoints only · PMID 31542391 · Corrigendum PMID 31982828. The course does not report doses.

citations.title: Topical rapamycin reduces markers of senescence and aging in human skin: an exploratory, prospective, randomized trial
citations.authors: Chung CL, Lawrence I, Hoffman M, et al.

note.en: exploratory placebo-controlled RCT; 36 enrolled, 19 discontinued or lost to follow-up (NCT03103893) · academic (Drexel University) · role: the one randomized study of a senomorphic in human skin found: p16 protein fell and collagen VII rose; clinical change described only in 'multiple participants' · PMID 31761958 · Not cited by either guide.

citations.title: Sunscreen and prevention of skin aging: a randomized trial
citations.authors: Hughes MC, Williams GM, Baker P, Green AC

note.en: community RCT (Nambour), n=903 adults under 55, 4.5 years, blinded assessors (ACTRN12610000086066) · public (National Health and Medical Research Council of Australia) · role: daily sunscreen: no detectable increase in skin ageing over 4.5 years and 24% less ageing than discretionary use · PMID 23732711 · Not cited by either guide (A&RE ch.10 recommends sun protection without a trial citation).

citations.title: Topical tretinoin for treating photoaging: A systematic review of randomized controlled trials
citations.authors: Sitohang IBS, Makes WI, Sandora N, Suryanegara J

note.en: systematic review of 7 RCTs · academic; no conflicts declared · role: the randomized-trial base behind the guide's GRADE A for topical retinoids in photoageing: consistent improvement in wrinkling, mottled pigmentation and lentigines · PMID 35620028 · A&RE gives no citation for its GRADE A; this review supplies one.

citations.title: Improvement of naturally aged skin with vitamin A (retinol)
citations.authors: Kafi R, Kwak HS, Schumacher WE, et al.

note.en: randomized double-blind vehicle-controlled arm comparison, n=36, mean age 87, 24 weeks · academic (NIH-supported) · role: retinol improved fine wrinkling of naturally aged skin; biopsy subgroups showed more glycosaminoglycan and procollagen I · PMID 17515510 · Not cited by either guide. Concentrations are not reported by the course.

citations.title: Vitamin A antagonizes decreased cell growth and elevated collagen-degrading matrix metalloproteinases and stimulates collagen accumulation in naturally aged human skin
citations.authors: Varani J, Warner RL, Gharaee-Kermani M, et al.

note.en: human sun-protected skin by age group (n=72) plus one-week topical retinol in 53 people aged 80+ · academic · role: aged skin shows more MMPs and less collagen synthesis; one week of topical retinol lowered MMPs and raised collagen synthesis · PMID 10692106 · Not cited by either guide. Concentrations are not reported by the course.

citations.title: Localization, age- and site-dependent expression, and regulation of 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 1 in skin
citations.authors: Tiganescu A, Walker EA, Hardy RS, Mayes AE, Stewart PM

note.en: human skin explants and primary dermal fibroblasts; mouse skin · academic (University of Birmingham) · role: keratinocytes and dermal fibroblasts express 11β-HSD1 (not 11β-HSD2); activity rises with donor age; photo-exposed fibroblasts express more; glucocorticoid availability is regulated at a pre-receptor level, independently of systemic levels · PMID 20739946 · A&RE ch.8 ref 2; verified

citations.title: 11β-Hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase blockade prevents age-induced skin structure and function defects
citations.authors: Tiganescu A, Tahrani AA, Morgan SA, et al.

note.en: human skin biopsies (young vs older; photo-exposed vs photo-protected) + 11β-HSD1 knockout mice · academic (University of Birmingham) · role: 11β-HSD1 activity elevated in aged and photo-exposed human skin; knockout mice protected from age-induced dermal atrophy; physiological cortisol inhibits collagen biosynthesis in dermal fibroblasts · PMID 23722901 · not cited by the guides; open access PMC3696573

citations.title: Oral 11β-HSD1 inhibitor AZD4017 improves wound healing and skin integrity in adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus: a pilot randomized controlled trial
citations.authors: Ajjan RA, Hensor EMA, Del Galdo F, et al.

note.en: statutory instrument · legislation · role: UK specials: regulation 46 does not apply to a 'special medicinal product' supplied in response to an unsolicited order, manufactured to the specification of a doctor, dentist, nurse independent prescriber, pharmacist independent prescriber or supplementary prescriber, for a patient for whose treatment that person is directly responsible, to fulfil the patient's special needs; condition B: no advertisement may be published; condition E: UK manufacture by the holder of a manufacturer's licence relating specifically to special medicinal products · Fetched live and read 2026-09-25 (HTTP 200).

citations.title: Medicines Act 1968, section 10 — Exemptions for pharmacists
citations.publication: legislation.gov.uk · latest available (revised) text, stated up to date to 25 September 2026

note.en: statute · legislation · role: UK: the restrictions of regulations 17(1) (manufacture) and 46 (authorisation) of the 2012 Regulations do not apply to preparing or dispensing a medicinal product in a registered pharmacy, hospital, care home service or health centre, by or under the supervision of a pharmacist, in accordance with a prescription given by an appropriate practitioner · Fetched live and read 2026-09-25 (HTTP 200).

citations.title: Good practice in proposing, prescribing, providing and managing medicines and devices — Prescribing unlicensed medicines (paragraphs 102–108)
citations.publication: gmc-uk.org · in effect 5 April 2021, updated 15 March 2022 and 13 December 2024

note.en: professional standard · statutory professional regulator · role: UK doctors: GMC uses 'unlicensed medicine' for medicines used outside their UK licence or with no UK licence (102); usually prescribe licensed medicines within their licence (103); when prescribing an unlicensed medicine, be satisfied there is sufficient evidence or experience of safety and efficacy, take responsibility for prescribing and for overseeing care, monitoring and follow-up, and record the reasons where not following common practice (105); explain to the patient, with reasons, when use is not routine or licensed alternatives exist (108) · Read in a browser 2026-09-25; gmc-uk.org answers scripts with HTTP 403, so the automated source check cannot read it.

citations.title: In practice: Guidance for pharmacist prescribers (updated April 2025)

note.en: professional standard · statutory professional regulator · role: UK pharmacist prescribers: a pharmacist independent prescriber may prescribe any medicine for any condition within their scope and competence (exceptions: three controlled drugs for addiction and initiating unlicensed cannabis-based products); for an unlicensed or off-label medicine they must be sure of sufficient evidence and experience of its safety and effectiveness, and record discussions and the reasons for prescribing decisions · Fetched live and read 2026-09-25 (HTTP 200). PDF read in the sections used.

citations.title: The Code: professional standards of practice and behaviour for nurses, midwives and nursing associates — standard 18

note.en: professional standard · statutory professional regulator · role: UK nurses and midwives: advise on, prescribe, supply, dispense or administer medicines within the limits of training and competence, the law, NMC guidance and other relevant policies (18); prescribe only with enough knowledge of the person's health and when satisfied the treatment serves their health needs (18.1); only registrants with a recorded prescribing qualification may prescribe · Fetched live and read 2026-09-25 (HTTP 200).

citations.title: The Human Medicines Regulations 2012 (SI 2012/1916), regulation 284 — Prescription only medicines (advertising)
citations.publication: legislation.gov.uk · latest available (revised) text, stated up to date to 25 September 2026

note.en: statutory instrument · legislation · role: UK: a person may not publish an advertisement that is likely to lead to the use of a prescription only medicine (exceptions only for approved vaccination and pathogen-spread campaigns) · Fetched live and read 2026-09-25 (HTTP 200).

citations.title: UK Code of Non-broadcast Advertising and Direct & Promotional Marketing (CAP Code), Section 12 — Medicines, medical devices, health-related products and beauty products
citations.authors: Committee of Advertising Practice / Advertising Standards Authority

note.en: advertising code · self-regulatory body backed by statutory referral · role: UK advertising: objective claims must be backed by evidence, where relevant trials on people (12.1); medicines must hold a licence before they are marketed (12.11); prescription-only medicines or prescription-only medical treatments may not be advertised to the public (12.12) · Fetched live and read 2026-09-25 (HTTP 200).

citations.title: Blue Guide: advertising and promotion of medicines in the UK (2020 edition)
citations.authors: Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (UK)
citations.publication: gov.uk · PDF, 116 pp · page last updated 28 March 2025

note.en: regulator guidance · regulator · role: UK advertising: medicinal products without a valid licence may not be advertised (regulation 279, s. 4.2); specials suppliers may not advertise specific unlicensed products; clinics may promote their service, e.g. 'treatment for lines and wrinkles', but must not name prescription-only products such as 'Botox' (s. 7.3); in treatment-service websites and social media, unlicensed medicines should not be mentioned, treatments using them may not be called 'clinically proven', and naming a prescription-only medicine in a clinic's social media is likely to be a prohibited advertisement (Appendix 6) · Fetched live and read 2026-09-25 (HTTP 200). PDF read in the sections used.

citations.title: ASA Ruling on Menwell Ltd t/a Voy (complaint A25-1295306)

note.en: advertising ruling · self-regulatory body backed by statutory referral · role: UK: four Instagram posts by customers of an online pharmacy's refer-a-friend scheme, with discount codes and hashtags such as '#mounjaro' and 'glp1', were ads under the pharmacy's control that promoted a prescription-only medicine to the public, breaching CAP Code rule 12.12; part of the ASA's wider work on weight-loss POMs · Fetched live and read 2026-09-25 (HTTP 200).

citations.title: Guidance for doctors who offer cosmetic interventions — Safety and quality (paragraphs 7–13)
citations.publication: gmc-uk.org · in effect 1 June 2016, updated 13 December 2024

note.en: professional standard · statutory professional regulator · role: UK doctors offering cosmetic interventions must carry out a physical examination before prescribing injectable cosmetic medicines and must not prescribe them by telephone, video link, online or at the request of others for patients they have not examined (11); interventions must rest on the best available evidence about effectiveness, side effects and risks (12) · Read in a browser 2026-09-25; gmc-uk.org answers scripts with HTTP 403, so the automated source check cannot read it.

modules.title: The skin as an endocrine organ, and how it ages
modules.titleEn: The skin as an endocrine organ, and how it ages
modules.objective: By the end, you can analyze the autonomous neuro-immuno-endocrine physiology of the skin and evaluate how local steroidogenesis, receptor expression, and cellular senescence drive structural dermal aging.

units.title: The skin as an endocrine organ, and how it ages

blocks.title: The skin makes its own hormones.
blocks.narration: This course starts with physiology, because every later question about a hormone or peptide for skin rests on it. Skin senses hormones from the blood, makes several of its own, and ages in ways that change both. In three lessons you will separate what happens locally in the skin from what the rest of the body sends in, and label each finding by the kind of evidence behind it.

blocks.title: The skin as an endocrine organ, and how it ages
blocks.sourceNote: Slominski 2025 · Slominski & Wortsman 2000 · Zouboulis 2004 · Roosterman 2006 · Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 5–6

blocks.title: How will you use this course?
blocks.narration: The evidence and grades are the same for everyone, and regulatory notes follow the country you choose. What changes with your role, in every module, is the 'what you do next' at the end of each lesson, so it fits what your licence lets you do.

blocks.title: Four units, one circuit.
blocks.narration: Think of the skin as a sensing organ with its own hormone supply. Researchers who study it describe four units, epidermal, dermal, hypodermal and adnexal, the last meaning hair follicles and glands. Each unit holds cells that can make hormones and mount an immune response, such as keratinocytes, fibroblasts, sebocytes, fat cells and mast cells. Signals move three ways. Neighbouring cells talk directly, sensory nerves carry messages in and out, and some products enter the blood and reach distant organs. Keep one distinction in view for the whole module. A signal that is made and used inside the skin is a local loop. A hormone that arrives from the blood, or leaves the skin for the rest of the body, is systemic signalling. Much of what follows is mechanism, drawn from cell, tissue and animal studies, and each finding will be labelled that way.
blocks.sourceNote: Slominski 2025 · Slominski & Wortsman 2000 · Zouboulis 2004 · Roosterman 2006 · Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 5–6

blocks.title: A steroid factory with local axes.
blocks.narration: Skin cells carry the enzymes to build steroids from cholesterol or to activate precursors arriving in the blood, and they run shortened copies of the body's central hormone axes. Each row names the evidence it rests on, because most of it comes from cells, tissue kept alive outside the body, or mice.
blocks.sourceNote: Slominski 2013 · Ito 2005 · Phan 2021 · Mancino 2021 · Horesh 2023 · Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 6

blocks.title: Three directions of traffic.
blocks.narration: Hormone signals in skin run in three directions. Some are made and used in the same patch of skin. Some arrive from the blood. A few leave the skin and act on the rest of the body. Knowing which one you are looking at decides whether the answer lies in the skin or in a systemic assessment.
blocks.sourceNote: Slominski 2025 · Phan 2021 · Ito 2005 · Holick 1980 · Bikle 2014 · Safer 2011 · Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 5–7

blocks.title: Read the skin before the serum.
blocks.narration: Picture the consultation where a patient asks about thinning, bruising skin. The Aesthetic and Regenerative Endocrinology guide asks you to read that skin as a window on the whole endocrine system before reaching for a serum. Sudden thinning with easy bruising suggests cortisol excess. Coarse, dry, cool skin suggests an underactive thyroid. New acanthosis nigricans points to insulin resistance. The guide lists violaceous striae with new hypertension or diabetes, rapidly progressive virilisation, and signs of an endocrine tumour as reasons to refer promptly to endocrinology. The local loops from the last two moments explain how skin behaves day to day. They are foundation biology, and the guide is explicit that they are no rationale for dosing anyone with a hormone. Whatever your role, a systemic pattern in the skin gets a systemic answer.
blocks.sourceNote: Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 5 clinical pearl and referral list · Safer 2011

blocks.title: 'My skin makes its own cortisol.'
blocks.narration: One question to close lesson 1.1.
blocks.sourceNote: Lesson 1.1

quiz.prompt: Fictional case. A 52-year-old has new thin, easily bruised skin on her forearms, new violaceous striae and newly raised blood pressure. She has read that skin makes its own cortisol and asks whether a cream could calm it. Which reading is right?

blocks.title: A map of fourteen million cells.
blocks.narration: Fourteen million cells is the scale of the Hormone Cell Atlas, a Cambridge-led study published in Science in 2026. The team read the RNA for 379 hormone and receptor genes in single cells and nuclei from forty-seven human tissues, skin included. From those readings they scored each cell type for its predicted capacity to make or to receive a hormone, and they flagged unexpected sites, such as RNA for the gut hormone secretin in a type of immune cell. The Aesthetic and Regenerative Endocrinology guide uses the atlas to argue that the skin, built from every major cell lineage, is plausibly one of the body's largest distributed signalling networks. The word plausibly matters. Everything in the atlas starts from RNA, and RNA tells you what a cell could make. Whether the cell actually makes and releases the hormone is the question the rest of this lesson answers.
blocks.sourceNote: Fei & Huang-Doran et al., Science 2026 · hormonecellatlas.org.uk · Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 7

blocks.title: Prediction, in the authors' own words.
blocks.narration: The atlas's own portal describes its scores as 'putative and hypothesis-generating'. A few predictions were tested in cells in the paper itself; the rest are left for users to validate. Across biology, the amount of RNA for a gene is often a poor guide to how much protein a cell makes, and protein is still a step short of secretion.
blocks.sourceNote: Fei & Huang-Doran, Science 2026 · hormonecellatlas.org.uk About/FAQ, read 24 Sep 2026 · Liu 2016

stat.label: hormone and receptor genes read as RNA, cell by cell

blocks.title: Transcript, tissue or person?
blocks.narration: Findings about skin as an endocrine organ sit on different rungs of the same ladder. Before you see the answers, decide how far up each one reaches.
blocks.sourceNote: Fei 2026 · atlas portal · Ito 2005 · Phan 2021 · Horesh 2023 · Holick 1980 · Bikle 2014

blocks.title: A map to confirm, then a trial.
blocks.narration: Two habits follow from the atlas. The first concerns product claims. Topical and transdermal treatments act through receptors the skin already carries, and the skin's own enzymes change how strongly a hormone acts once it arrives, so the response in skin can differ from what the dose predicts. A receptor on a map is where an efficacy question starts, and the answer still needs a trial. The second habit concerns the physiology you think you know. The guide's testing pearl says serum vitamin D falls with sunscreen use, which the biology predicts. An independent review found that in real-life field trials, daily sunscreen did not lower blood levels, although the sunscreens tested were moderate and today's high-protection products have never been trialled. Keep recommending sun protection, and treat vitamin D as its own question.
blocks.sourceNote: Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 6–7 pearls · Neale 2019 · Fei 2026 · Bikle 2014

blocks.title: 'Your skin has receptors for it.'
blocks.narration: One question to close lesson 1.2.
blocks.sourceNote: Lesson 1.2

quiz.prompt: A brochure for a hormone-containing serum cites a single-cell atlas showing that dermal fibroblasts carry the RNA for that hormone's receptor. What does that finding establish?

blocks.title: Cells that stop dividing and keep talking.
blocks.narration: Senescence begins as a safety mechanism. A cell that has taken enough damage stops dividing for good, which helps guard against cancer and is useful during wound repair. The problem is what the cell does next. It stays alive and metabolically busy and releases a mixture of inflammatory cytokines such as interleukin six and eight, enzymes that break down matrix, and growth factors. This secretory profile, the SASP, was characterised in human cells grown in the laboratory after DNA damage. In living human skin, the evidence is observational. Skin samples from older people contain more cells carrying the senescence marker p16, in both the epidermis and the dermis, and fibroblasts, keratinocytes and melanocytes can all become senescent. Researchers also caution that no single marker identifies a senescent cell with certainty, so counts depend on the marker chosen.
blocks.sourceNote: Coppé 2008 · Ressler 2006 · Ho & Dreesen 2021 · Wang & Dreesen 2018 · Haykal 2026 · Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 7

blocks.title: Three years of perceived age.
blocks.narration: In a Dutch cohort, people with more p16-positive cells in sun-protected arm skin had more ageing-type elastic fibres, more facial wrinkles and looked older, after allowing for their actual age. The epidermal p16-positive cells were mostly melanocytes. The study was publicly funded; one co-author worked for Unilever.
blocks.sourceNote: Waaijer 2016 (Leiden Longevity Study) · Ressler 2006

stat.label: younger-looking: fewest versus most p16-positive epidermal cells, at the same chronological age

blocks.title: Human, mouse or dish?
blocks.narration: Senescence research mixes human tissue, mice and cultured cells. For the ageing dermis the four answers point in different directions, which is why they belong in separate sentences.
blocks.sourceNote: Shuster 1975 · Varani 2006 · Fisher 2009 · Waaijer 2016 · Baker 2016 · Xu 2018 · Hickson 2019 · Chung 2019

blocks.title: The levers with trials behind them.
blocks.narration: Set the senescence story beside the interventions that have been tested in people. In Nambour, Australia, a publicly funded trial randomised 903 adults to daily or discretionary sunscreen, and over four and a half years skin ageing was about a quarter lower with daily use. Topical tretinoin has a run of randomised trials in photoaged skin that agree with one another, and the Aesthetic and Regenerative Endocrinology guide rates topical retinoids first-line, grade A. Retinol has smaller trials, including one in residents in their late eighties whose fine wrinkling improved and whose biopsies showed more procollagen. Both levers protect or rebuild the dermal matrix that ultraviolet light and, it is thought, the SASP erode, and both have human outcome data. Senolytics for skin have no such data yet. Keep that order in mind when a patient asks what actually works.
blocks.sourceNote: Hughes 2013 · Sitohang 2022 · Kafi 2007 · Varani 2000 · Fisher 2002 · Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 5

blocks.title: 'Can a senolytic fix my skin?'
blocks.narration: Consider a fifty-eight-year-old patient, fictional and built from this lesson's evidence. She has read that senolytic supplements clear so-called zombie cells and reverse skin ageing, and she asks whether to start one she found online. She does not wear sunscreen every day. Three facts frame the conversation. Senescent cells really do accumulate in human skin, and their number tracks with wrinkles and with how old a person looks. The evidence that clearing them helps comes from mice, and the human studies so far are small pilots measuring markers in tissue. Daily sunscreen and topical retinoids, by contrast, have randomised trials with visible skin outcomes. The Aesthetic and Regenerative Endocrinology guide advises keeping senolytics within clinical trials. Decide what you say first.
blocks.sourceNote: Fictional case · Waaijer 2016 · Baker 2016 · Hickson 2019 · Hughes 2013 · Sitohang 2022 · Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 17

blocks.title: Mouse, human, or both?
blocks.narration: One question to close lesson 1.3.
blocks.sourceNote: Lesson 1.3

quiz.prompt: Which statement about senescence and skin ageing matches the evidence?

blocks.title: Before my next skin-and-hormone conversation.
blocks.narration: Build the checklist you will actually use. It is saved to your path and your tutor will bring it back.
blocks.sourceNote: Module 01

check.prompt: Closing Module 1 (fictional case). A 41-year-old with a low serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D says she will stop sunscreen because 'skin makes vitamin D'. Which reply keeps the physiology and the evidence straight?

options.text: Vitamin D made in skin stays in the skin, so sunscreen cannot affect her blood level.
Skin synthesis does feed her blood level, but field trials of daily sunscreen did not lower 25-hydroxyvitamin D; keep sun protection and treat the low level as its own clinical question.
The guide says sunscreen lowers vitamin D, so stopping it is reasonable.

modules.title: Systemic hormones and the skin
modules.objective: By the end, you can differentiate cutaneous manifestations of systemic endocrine disorders from localized hormonal aging, appraising the clinical limitations and risks of hormone replacement in skin health.

blocks.title: The face that might be a diagnosis.
blocks.narration: Most skin changes you see are ageing or lifestyle. A few are the first visible sign of endocrine disease. In three lessons you will separate them: what local and systemic hormones do to skin, what hormone therapy can and cannot do for it, and which signs belong with an endocrinologist.

blocks.title: Systemic hormones and the skin
blocks.sourceNote: Slominski & Wortsman 2000 · Tiganescu 2011, 2013 · Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 8

blocks.title: The skin regenerates its own cortisol.
blocks.narration: Picture the skin as a small endocrine organ with its own stress axis. Skin cells make CRH and ACTH, the same signals that drive the adrenal glands, and they carry the receptors to respond to them. They also carry an enzyme called eleven beta HSD one, which turns inactive cortisone back into active cortisol inside the cell. In human skin samples that enzyme works harder with age and in sun-exposed skin, and it sets local cortisol independently of the level in the blood. Cortisol slows collagen production in dermal fibroblasts, and mice bred without the enzyme kept their dermal thickness as they aged. Hold all of this in the mechanism register. It comes from biopsies, cultured cells and mice, and it says nothing yet about how a patient's face will age.
blocks.sourceNote: Slominski & Wortsman 2000 · Tiganescu 2011, 2013 · Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 8

blocks.title: 11β-HSD1: four separate answers.
blocks.narration: Local cortisol regeneration is a real and interesting mechanism. Each register below answers a different question, and blending them produces the line you will hear online: that blocking cortisol in the skin reverses ageing.
blocks.sourceNote: Tiganescu 2011, 2013 · Ajjan 2022 · ClinicalTrials.gov and Drugs@FDA, checked 24 Sep 2026

blocks.title: Which features point to Cushing's?
blocks.narration: Cushing's syndrome shares most of its features with ordinary weight gain, poor sleep and stress. The Endocrine Society's diagnostic guideline separates the few that discriminate from the many that are common. Before you see its verdicts, sort these eight.
blocks.sourceNote: Endocrine Society guideline, Nieman 2008, Table 1 · Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 8

blocks.title: Rare, and usually from a prescription.
blocks.narration: Endogenous Cushing's syndrome is uncommon: European population studies put it at two to three new cases per million people a year. The commonest cause of Cushing's syndrome is iatrogenic, from glucocorticoids given as medicine. The Endocrine Society therefore asks for a drug history first, covering tablets, inhalers, injections and creams, including skin-bleaching products, and recommends testing when features are multiple and progressive.
blocks.sourceNote: Endocrine Society guideline, Nieman 2008 — introduction and recommendations 3.1–3.3

stat.label: new cases of endogenous Cushing's syndrome per million people per year (European population studies)

blocks.title: Reassure the many, refer the few.
blocks.narration: Here is how that plays out when a patient asks about cortisol face. Begin with a drug history, because the commonest cause of cortisol excess is a glucocorticoid someone is already using. The guideline names the easy ones to miss, such as skin-bleaching creams, herbal tonics, and joint or nerve injections. Then look for the four features that shift the odds, meaning easy bruising, a plethoric face, weakness in the hips and shoulders, and wide reddish-purple striae. Without them, the Aesthetic and Regenerative Endocrinology guide reads most puffiness as sleep, alcohol, salt and fluid, and the Endocrine Society advises against testing everyone. With them, and especially when they are progressing, the patient needs formal testing and an endocrinologist. A cortisol supplement or a mail-order saliva panel answers the wrong question.
blocks.sourceNote: Endocrine Society guideline 2008, recommendations 3.1–3.5 · Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 8 clinical pearl

blocks.title: 'Is this cortisol face?'
blocks.narration: One question to close lesson 2.1.
blocks.sourceNote: Lesson 2.1

quiz.prompt: A 38-year-old asks whether her puffy morning face is 'cortisol face'. She sleeps badly and drinks most evenings. What is the best next step?

blocks.title: Estrogen and the dermis.
blocks.narration: Estrogen is the hormone the guide says dominates the visible ageing of women's skin, so start with what it does in the dermis. Skin carries estrogen receptors in sun-protected and sun-damaged sites alike. In a vehicle-controlled study, two weeks of topical estradiol raised collagen production in the hip skin of postmenopausal women; in photoaged forearm and facial skin, the same treatment made no measurable difference. Small biopsy studies from the nineteen eighties and nineties found that skin collagen and thickness fall after menopause, and that the fall follows years since the last period more closely than birthdays. Keep two questions apart as you go. One is what estrogen does in the dermis. The other is whether giving it changes how a face ages, and those answers come from different trials.
blocks.sourceNote: Rittié 2008 · Thornton 2013 · Brincat 1985 · Affinito 1999 · Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 9

blocks.title: One to two per cent a year.
blocks.narration: In small biopsy studies of postmenopausal women, skin collagen content and skin thickness fell by about 1–2% a year, in step with bone mass, and followed years since menopause more than age. Reviews, and the Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide, quote a steeper early loss of up to 30% in the first five years. That figure traces to the same small studies, and a check of their abstracts in September 2026 did not find it stated.
blocks.sourceNote: Brincat 1985, 1987 · Affinito 1999 · Thornton 2013

stat.label: fall in skin collagen content and thickness per year after menopause (small biopsy studies)

blocks.title: Biopsy gains, mirror results.
blocks.narration: Hormone therapy has two kinds of trial behind it. Small trials measure the dermis; larger trials measure the face. They point in different directions, so read them separately. The Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide grades the skin benefit B; the North American Menopause Society rates the same evidence 'limited or inconsistent'. This course grades the structural gains C and teaches the negative wrinkle trials alongside them.
blocks.sourceNote: Maheux 1994 · Sauerbronn 2000 · Phillips 2008 · Owen 2016 · Pivazyan 2023 · Creidi 1994 · Ashcroft 1999 · NAMS 2022

blocks.title: Symptoms and bone. Skin is a bystander.
blocks.narration: Where does that leave hormone therapy for skin? In the United States, as of February 2026, the approved uses of menopausal hormone therapy are hot flashes, vaginal and vulvar symptoms, and for some products the prevention of bone loss. In late 2025 the FDA asked manufacturers to remove heart, breast cancer and dementia statements from the boxed warning, and it approved the first revised labels in February 2026. Skin still appears nowhere among the uses. The menopause society's 2022 position statement finds the balance favourable for symptoms and bone when therapy starts before sixty or within ten years of menopause, and it finds too little evidence for compounded bioidentical hormones. Low-dose vaginal estrogen for genitourinary symptoms is the one use aimed at the tissue itself. For the face, daily sunscreen and a prescription retinoid carry better evidence than any hormone. Treat symptoms on their merits, and count any skin change as a bonus.
blocks.sourceNote: FDA, 10 Nov 2025 and 12 Feb 2026 · 21 CFR 310.530 · NAMS 2022, 2020 · Manson 2013 · Hughes 2013 · Renova label · UK: Evorel and Sandrena SmPCs, MHRA Guidance Note 14, medicines compendium (checked 25 Sep 2026)

blocks.title: 'Hormones for my skin.'
blocks.narration: One question to close lesson 2.2.
blocks.sourceNote: Lesson 2.2

quiz.prompt: A 52-year-old with no hot flashes, no sleep disturbance and no vaginal symptoms asks for estrogen 'to stop my face ageing'. What does the evidence support?

blocks.title: Some syndromes show on the skin first.
blocks.narration: Some endocrine syndromes are written on the skin years before the glands give them away. In multiple endocrine neoplasia type one, most patients in one careful series had several facial angiofibromas, the same lesions seen in tuberous sclerosis, along with collagenomas on the trunk. In Carney complex, usually caused by inactivating variants in the PRKAR1A gene, freckle-like lentigines cluster on the lips, eyelids and the corners of the eyes, alongside blue naevi and small skin myxomas. The same patients can develop myxomas in the heart and cortisol-secreting adrenal disease. In MEN two A, an itchy, rippled, darkened patch between the shoulder blades, called cutaneous lichen amyloidosis, can appear long before medullary thyroid cancer. Each of these is a referral finding, and none of them is yours to diagnose alone.
blocks.sourceNote: Darling 1997 · Kirschner 2000 · Correa 2015 · Stanescu 2024 · Lause 2017 · the guide's inherited-syndromes chapter

blocks.title: Eighty-eight per cent.
blocks.narration: In a consecutive series of 32 people with MEN1 examined at the US National Institutes of Health, 88% had multiple facial angiofibromas and 72% had collagenomas. The angiofibromas were clinically and histologically identical to those of tuberous sclerosis. The authors concluded that angiofibromas in someone without tuberous sclerosis call for biochemical testing for MEN1.
blocks.sourceNote: Darling et al., Arch Dermatol 1997

stat.label: of 32 people with MEN1 had multiple facial angiofibromas

blocks.title: The everyday endocrine signs.
blocks.narration: Most of the endocrine skin signs you will actually meet come from common conditions. New, generalised darkening, most obvious in skin creases such as the palms, in scars, on the gums and on sun-exposed skin, can be the sign of primary adrenal insufficiency. In a patient who is also unwell, the Endocrine Society recommends testing, and a suspected adrenal crisis is treated before the results come back, because delay raises the risk of death. Hirsutism that arrives quickly, keeps progressing, or comes with a deeper voice or clitoromegaly makes an androgen-secreting tumour more likely and calls for prompt referral. Velvety dark plaques in the neck folds track insulin resistance. Firm plaques on the shins point to Graves' disease, and cold, dry, coarse skin suggests an underactive thyroid. The skin shows you which door to knock on.
blocks.sourceNote: Endocrine Society guidelines: Bornstein 2016, Martin 2018 · Lause 2017 · the guide's ch. 5 referral list

blocks.title: Where does this skin finding go?

blocks.title: Freckles before the wedding.
blocks.narration: Consider a fictional patient, built from this lesson's evidence. She is twenty-nine and wants the freckles on her lips and at the corners of her eyes lasered before her wedding. While you examine her you notice a soft, skin-coloured bump on one eyelid. She mentions that her father had a heart tumour removed in his thirties. Pigmented spots at the corners of the eyes are seen in Carney complex and Peutz–Jeghers syndrome, and small skin myxomas favour the eyelids and ears. In Carney complex, tumours of the heart cause more than half of the deaths, which is why screening matters once the diagnosis is suspected. The laser itself may be harmless. The question is what the skin is telling you. Choose your first move.
blocks.sourceNote: Correa 2015 · Kirschner 2000 · the guide's inherited-syndromes chapter

Estrogen acts on skin receptors (mechanism); small trials show thicker skin, while the largest found no wrinkle difference (evidence); US approved uses are symptoms and bone (regulation); whether longer treatment changes facial ageing is untested (open question).

units.title: Fat, incretins and the ageing face

blocks.title: The face changes when the fat does.
blocks.narration: Facial shape depends on fat as much as on collagen. In three lessons you will separate what is known about the skin's own fat, sugar damage to the dermis, weight-loss drugs and the gut from what is still mechanism, marketing or an open question.

blocks.title: Fat, incretins and the ageing face
blocks.sourceNote: Zhang 2015, 2019 · Chen 2019 · Kruglikov & Scherer 2016 · O'Neill 2022 · Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 11

blocks.title: The skin keeps its own fat.
blocks.narration: Most people picture skin fat as one layer under the dermis. There is a second, thinner layer inside the reticular dermis itself, called dermal white adipose tissue. In mice, this layer expands rapidly after a Staphylococcus aureus infection, and its new fat cells release cathelicidin, an antimicrobial peptide. Older mice lose much of that capacity, through TGF-beta signalling. Human skin arranges this fat differently, in small cones around hair follicles, and human acne lesions contain preadipocytes around the follicle that make cathelicidin. What the layer contributes to human skin ageing has not yet been measured. So hold two things apart when you hear about skin fat. The defence story is strong in mice and emerging in people. The ageing story in people is still a proposal.
blocks.sourceNote: Zhang 2015, 2019 · Chen 2019 · Kruglikov & Scherer 2016 · O'Neill 2022 · Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 11

blocks.title: Fat that holds the face up.
blocks.narration: Cadaver dissection shows that the face's subcutaneous fat sits in separate compartments, and facial ageing is partly how each compartment changes. Weight shows the same thing from the outside. In a study of 186 pairs of identical twins, the twin with the higher body-mass index looked older before about age 40 and younger after it.
blocks.sourceNote: Rohrich & Pessa 2007 · Guyuron 2009

stat.label: pairs of identical twins compared for facial ageing

blocks.title: Sugar that sticks to collagen.
blocks.narration: Glycation is chemistry before it is biology. Reducing sugars attach to the amino groups of proteins, rearrange into more stable products, and end as advanced glycation end products, known as AGEs. Dermal collagen lasts for years, so it collects AGEs, and they form cross-links that make the matrix stiffer. AGEs also bind a receptor called RAGE, which in laboratory studies switches on inflammatory signalling and enzymes that break down matrix. Keep the registers apart here. The chemistry, and the build-up of AGEs in human skin, are well documented. The idea that AGEs cause the wrinkles and laxity you see in clinic rests on laboratory and animal work plus human associations. The Aesthetic and Regenerative Endocrinology guide rates the structural and inflammatory effects grade B. This course grades the causal link D, and the next moment shows why.
blocks.sourceNote: Gkogkolou & Böhm 2012 · Dyer 1993 · Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 13

blocks.title: Fifteen years on the same collagen.
blocks.narration: Human skin collagen turns over slowly; tissue analysis puts its half-life at about 15 years. In skin biopsies, glycoxidation products in collagen rose about five-fold between ages 20 and 85, and were up to twice as high in type 1 diabetes. Skin autofluorescence, a non-invasive reading, correlates moderately with those biopsy measures and was validated in non-pigmented skin.
blocks.sourceNote: Verzijl 2000 · Dyer 1993 · Meerwaldt 2004

stat.label: estimated half-life of human skin collagen

blocks.title: Mouse, human or marketing?
blocks.narration: Six statements you will hear about skin fat and glycation. Before you see where each one stands, decide what kind of evidence is behind it.
blocks.sourceNote: Zhang 2015, 2019 · O'Neill 2022 · Dyer 1993 · Verzijl 2000 · Draelos 2025

quiz.prompt: A patient shows you her skin autofluorescence reading, lower after eight weeks on an 'anti-glycation' supplement. What does that result show?

blocks.title: Two gut hormones, re-engineered.
blocks.narration: After a meal, the gut releases two hormones called incretins, GLP-1 and GIP. Both amplify insulin release when glucose is high, and GLP-1 also slows the stomach and reduces appetite. Native GLP-1 lasts only minutes in the blood before an enzyme breaks it down, so the drug molecules are engineered to last far longer. Semaglutide activates the GLP-1 receptor. Tirzepatide activates both the GIP and the GLP-1 receptors. Those are the mechanisms. The regulatory facts sit in a separate register. In the United States, as of September 2026, both molecules are FDA-approved drugs, sold under one brand name for type 2 diabetes and another for chronic weight management, with further indications for the heart, the liver and sleep apnoea. The face appears nowhere on those labels, and that is where this lesson begins.
blocks.sourceNote: Drucker 2018 · Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 12 · Peptide Pocket Guide · US labels

blocks.title: Approved for what, exactly?
blocks.narration: The facial changes in this lesson happen to people taking approved drugs for approved reasons. Know the indications, and their dates, before you discuss the side effects. Status below is for the US, from FDA records checked in September 2026.
blocks.sourceNote: US labels via DailyMed (2026) · Drugs@FDA · FDA, current 1 Sep 2026 · Ashraf 2024

blocks.title: Large trials, measured on the scale.
blocks.narration: In STEP-1, 1,961 adults without diabetes lost a mean 14.9% of body weight on semaglutide over 68 weeks, against 2.4% on placebo. In SURMOUNT-1, 2,539 adults lost 15.0% to 20.9% on tirzepatide over 72 weeks, depending on dose, against 3.1% on placebo. Both Hormonaly guides grade weight management A. Across 35 randomized trials of incretin drugs, a median of about 28% of the weight lost was muscle-related tissue.
blocks.sourceNote: Wilding 2021 · Jastreboff 2022 · Batsis 2026

stat.label: mean weight loss in STEP-1 (semaglutide, 68 weeks) and SURMOUNT-1 (tirzepatide, highest dose, 72 weeks)

blocks.title: 'Ozempic face', answer by answer.
blocks.narration: The phrase bundles four kinds of statement. Kept apart, they tell a patient far more than the headline does.
blocks.sourceNote: Sharma 2025 · Rao 2026 · Daneshgaran 2025 · US labels 2026 · Paschou 2025

blocks.title: Counsel before, record during, refer when asked.
blocks.narration: Three moments matter in practice. Before treatment starts, raise facial volume change and hair shedding as possibilities, especially with older patients, as the Hormonaly guide advises, and record that you did. During treatment, photograph the face with consent so that change is measured rather than remembered, and support the protein intake and resistance training the guide recommends to protect lean mass. When a patient asks for help with the face, refer to a qualified aesthetic or dermatology colleague. The published advice on restoring volume after drug-driven weight loss is expert opinion, the main consensus statement was developed with industry involvement, and randomized trials of fillers and devices in these patients are registered with no results yet. Whatever your role, decisions about the medicine itself stay with the prescriber and the patient.
blocks.sourceNote: Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 12, 14 · Nikolis 2025 · ClinicalTrials.gov, checked 24 Sep 2026

blocks.title: Ten months in, and unhappy with the mirror.
blocks.narration: Picture a fifty-eight-year-old patient, fictional and built from this lesson's evidence. She has taken semaglutide for obesity for ten months, prescribed by her physician, and has lost eighteen percent of her body weight. Her blood pressure and glucose have improved. She is distressed by hollow cheeks and new looseness along the jaw, and she is finding more hair in her brush. She asks whether she should stop the injections. Consider what the evidence says. In the studies so far, facial volume loss tracks the amount of weight lost. Hair loss is a labelled side effect, reported more often in women and linked to weight reduction. The drug was prescribed for a medical reason, and that reason is going well. Decide how you would answer her.
blocks.sourceNote: Sharma 2025 · Rao 2026 · Wegovy label 2026 · Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 12

blocks.title: What the evidence shows.
blocks.narration: One question to close lesson 3.2.

quiz.prompt: Which statement about facial change on semaglutide or tirzepatide matches the evidence as of September 2026?

blocks.title: Inflammation that comes with age.
blocks.narration: Ageing brings a slow rise in background inflammation, called inflammaging. It is low-grade and sterile, and in older adults higher IL-6 and C-reactive protein predict frailty, disability and death. One proposed source is the gut. In mice, a high-fat diet raises bacterial lipopolysaccharide in the blood, and infusing that endotoxin reproduces weight gain and insulin resistance. In twelve healthy men, a single high-fat meal raised plasma endotoxin within four hours. That is the mechanism usually called metabolic endotoxaemia, or leaky gut. The human evidence stops short of the skin. Measuring gut permeability is difficult, and a leading review concludes that it is still unproven whether restoring the barrier improves disease outside the gut. Hold that line as you look at what patients are sold.
blocks.sourceNote: Franceschi 2000 · Ferrucci & Fabbri 2018 · Cani 2007 · Erridge 2007 · Camilleri 2019

blocks.title: Thirty-nine trials of probiotics for eczema.
blocks.narration: An independent Cochrane review pooled 39 randomized trials, with 2,599 participants, of oral probiotics for eczema. Probiotics probably make little or no difference to patient-rated symptoms, and investigator-rated severity fell by less than the minimum clinically important difference. A 2024 European task-force meta-analysis in children without food allergy reported a significant fall in severity scores.
blocks.sourceNote: Makrgeorgou 2018 (Cochrane) · Vassilopoulou 2024 · Suez 2019

stat.label: in the Cochrane review of oral probiotics for treating eczema

blocks.title: What has been tested on skin?
blocks.narration: Six things patients bring you under the heading 'gut health for skin'. One at a time, decide what stands behind each.
blocks.sourceNote: Makrgeorgou 2018 · Parodi 2008 · Lebwohl 2026 · Faurschou 2015 · Reynolds 2019 · Depommier 2019

blocks.title: Diet first, a bottle last.
blocks.narration: Patients often link their skin to their gut. Start where the evidence is. Diet quality, treatment of metabolic disease and the established treatment for the skin condition itself all come first. Be careful with tests. A widely used commercial zonulin assay was shown to detect proteins other than zonulin, so a result cannot tell you whether a gut is leaky. Be careful with products too. Probiotics are strain-specific, and their effects on eczema are small at best. The Hormonaly guide gives the popular gut-repair stack of glutamine, zinc carnosine and BPC-157 a grade of D. As of September 2026, in the United States, BPC-157 remains off the 503A bulks list after the July advisory-committee review. Investigational peptides come last, if at all. Whatever your role, name the evidence type before you name the product.
blocks.sourceNote: Scheffler 2018 · Camilleri 2019 · Makrgeorgou 2018 (Cochrane) · Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 16 · FDA PCAC, July 2026 · 21 CFR 216.23
